title: An Introduction to Causal Inference - PMC - NIH
author: Complex Causal Inference Group /Various
snippet: A foundational introduction to causal inference methodology distinguishing causal from correlational claims, covering potential outcomes, counterfactuals, and structural equations. Explicitly addresses confounding, selection bias, and identification assumptions required to move beyond association.
notes: PMC peer-reviewed methods tutorial by a leading causal-inference scholar.

title: Natural Experiments: An Overview of Methods, Approaches, and
author: Craig A. M. et al.
organization: PMC / NIH (Annual Review of Public Health)
snippet: Overview of natural experiment methods, approaches, and contributions. Defines natural experiments, contrasts them with randomized trials and observational analyses, and explains how quasi-random variation supports causal claims with explicit assumptions about exchangeability and exclusion restriction.
notes: PMC methods paper on natural-experiment design — strong gap-fill for causal vs correlational distinction.

title: Capitalizing on Natural Experiments to Improve Our Understanding of
author: Souza R. G. et al.
snippet: Argues for capitalizing on natural experiments to improve understanding of population health interventions. Discusses threats to validity (confounding, regression to the mean), pre/post comparison pitfalls, and the role of counterfactual reasoning in supporting causal attribution.
notes: PMC article emphasizing when natural experiments do and do not support causal claims.

title: Difference-in-Differences for Health Policy and Practice - PMC
author: Wing C. et al.
organization: PMC / NIH (Annual Review of Public Health)
snippet: A 2024 methods primer on difference-in-differences (DiD) for health policy and practice. Explains parallel-trends assumption, two-way fixed effects, event-study plots, and sensitivity to pre-trend violations. Explicitly distinguishes causal policy effects from descriptive before/after comparisons.
notes: Recent DiD methods paper — strong causal-methods coverage.

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs in Epidemiology - PMC - NIH
author: Bor J. et al.
snippet: Tutorial on regression discontinuity designs (RDD) in epidemiology, explaining how threshold-based assignment enables causal inference near cutoffs. Discusses continuity assumptions, bandwidth selection, and external validity trade-offs (estimates local to the cutoff, limited generalizability beyond).
notes: PMC epidemiology methods paper — strong scope-qualifier patterns (local to cutoff).

title: [2002.02770] A Survey on Causal Inference
author: Guo R. et al.
snippet: A Survey on Causal Inference Methods (arXiv 2002.02770) reviews assumptions, frameworks, and algorithms for causal estimation from observational data. Covers propensity scores, matching, IV, DiD, and structural nested models, emphasizing that association does not imply causation without identifying assumptions.
notes: arXiv OA methodology survey; useful cross-disciplinary causal-inference review.

title: Difference-in-Differences Designs: A Practitioner's Guide
author: Roth G. et al.
snippet: A Practitioner's Guide to Difference-in-Differences Designs (arXiv 2503.13323) walks applied researchers through modern DiD estimators (Callaway-Sant'Anna, de Chaisemartin-D'Haultfoeuille, Sun-Abraham), highlighting when standard two-way fixed effects gives misleading causal estimates under staggered treatment timing.
notes: Recent arXiv DiD methods guide — strong on limitations of canonical DiD.

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics
author: Lee D. S., Lemieux T.
snippet: Lee and Lemieux's NBER working paper 'Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics' provides a foundational methodological survey. Explains validity conditions, graphical tests (McCrary density), and the interpretation that RDD estimates are local average treatment effects at the cutoff with limited external scope.
notes: NBER working paper; widely cited RDD methodology reference.

title: Instrumental Variables: An Econometrician's Perspective - NBER
author: Heckman J. J., Urzua S.
snippet: Heckman and Urzua's 'Instrumental Variables: An Econometrician's Perspective' (NBER w19983) critiques the local average treatment effect (LATE) interpretation, arguing that IV estimates are population-specific and may not correspond to policy-relevant causal parameters — explicit scope qualifiers throughout.
notes: NBER working paper by Nobel laureate; strong scope-qualifier language around IV.

title: THE OREGON HEALTH INSURANCE EXPERIMENT - PMC
author: Finkelstein A. et al.
snippet: Finkelstein et al. report findings from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, a Medicaid lottery that provided quasi-random assignment. Reports causal effects on health, financial strain, and utilization, explicitly noting limits: lottery participants were a low-income, uninsured population in Oregon circa 2008.
notes: Landmark randomized Medicaid expansion study — explicit population scope qualifiers.

title: Moving to Opportunity: an Experimental Study of  - PMC
author: Katz L. F., Kling J. R., Liebman J. B.
organization: PMC / NIH (American Journal of Public Health)
snippet: The Moving to Opportunity (MTO) demonstration randomly offered housing vouchers to low-income families to relocate from high-poverty neighborhoods. Reports heterogeneous causal effects on adult economic outcomes versus child long-term outcomes, with explicit scope qualifiers tied to neighborhood characteristics.
notes: MTO randomized housing voucher study — classic causal-estimate source with scope language.

title: Causal inference in economics and marketing
author: Varian H. R.
snippet: PNAS perspective on causal inference in economics and marketing. Reviews quasi-experimental designs (DiD, RDD, IV, synthetic control) and discusses threats to identification; emphasizes that credible causal claims require transparent assumption disclosure and falsification tests.
notes: PNAS OA methodology paper.

title: Using natural experiments to evaluate population health and  - The BMJ
author: Pearce N. et al.
snippet: BMJ analysis on using natural experiments to evaluate population health and policy interventions. Reviews credibility levers (as-if random assignment, parallel trends, pre-registered analysis plans) and emphasizes that even strong natural experiments yield local causal estimates with bounded generalizability.
notes: BMJ OA article; strong on scope + attribution language.

title: Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast Food
author: Card D., Krueger A. B.
snippet: Card and Krueger's classic NBER working paper 'Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania' uses a natural experiment (NJ minimum wage increase) with DiD analysis. Reports no significant employment reduction — a landmark null finding in labor economics.
notes: Card-Krueger landmark DiD study — bridges causal + negative gaps.

title: Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging  - Nature
author: Bloom N. et al.
snippet: Nature (2024) reports a randomized controlled trial on hybrid working from home at Trip.com. Finds a 33% reduction in quit rates with no significant productivity loss — a causal estimate from a true experiment with explicit scope to knowledge workers at one firm.
notes: Nature OA RCT — bridges causal + negative findings + scope.

title: Why null results do not mean no results: negative findings
author: Bastian H. et al.
snippet: Examines why null results do not mean no results: argues that non-significant findings carry evidentiary value and should be reported with effect sizes, confidence intervals, and explicit descriptions of the populations and conditions under which no effect was detected.
notes: PMC paper explicitly framing the meaning of null results — strong negative-findings gap fill.

title: Reporting and interpretation of results from clinical trials that did not claim
author: Gewandter J. S. et al.
snippet: Studies reporting and interpretation of results from clinical trials that did not claim significance. Quantifies how often 'no significant difference' is misreported as 'no difference' — a methodological failure mode producing false-negative framing in the literature.
notes: PMC meta-research paper on misinterpreted null trial results.

title: Evidence of Lack of Treatment Efficacy Derived From Statistically  - PMC
author: Sedgwick P.
snippet: Examines how statistically non-significant efficacy results are framed, finding widespread 'absence of evidence' conflated with 'evidence of absence'. Discusses underpowered trials, confidence intervals crossing the null, and the importance of pre-specified minimum clinically important differences.
notes: PMC paper on interpretation of null trial efficacy results.

title: Promoting Learning from Null or Negative Results in  - PMC
author: Rohrig B. et al.
snippet: Discusses promoting learning from null or negative results in prevention science. Argues for publication of null findings to combat publication bias and for richer reporting of context, sample, and conditions to enable synthesis of when interventions do not produce expected effects.
notes: PMC article on publishing null prevention-science findings.

title: Promoting Learning from Null or Negative Results in Prevention
author: Sedgwick P. et al.
snippet: Springer paper on promoting learning from null or negative results in prevention research. Reviews editorial, methodological, and cultural barriers to publishing nulls; recommends registered reports, pre-analysis plans, and explicit discussion of contextual scope when reporting non-significant findings.
notes: Springer OA prevention-science paper — same theme as PMC7398716.

title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
author: Open Science Collaboration
snippet: Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Science paper 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science' replicated 100 published psychology studies. Found that only 36% showed statistically significant effects in replication — a landmark negative-finding meta-result on the field itself, with explicit scope qualifiers.
notes: Landmark reproducibility study — bridges negative + scope.

title: Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in
author: Camerer C. F. et al.
snippet: Camerer et al. (Nature Human Behaviour 2018) replicated 16 social-science experiments published in top journals. Found significant effect in the original direction for only 7, with effect sizes ~50% smaller — explicit null and replication-failure results with discussion of scope and power.
notes: Camerer social-science replication study — natural companion to OSC 2015.

title: Position: Embracing Negative Results in Machine Learning
author: Bouthillier F. et al.
snippet: arXiv 2406.03980 position paper 'Embracing Negative Results in Machine Learning'. Argues for systematic publication of null findings to combat over-optimism in ML benchmark leaderboards, with discussion of statistical power, multiple-comparison corrections, and conditions under which negative results are informative.
notes: arXiv OA position paper on negative results in ML.

title: Reproducibility in Machine Learning-based Research
author: Pineau J. et al.
snippet: arXiv 2406.14325 'Reproducibility in Machine Learning-based Research'. Reviews failures to replicate headline ML results, code-availability gaps, and the role of random seed variance; discusses sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification as aids to reproducibility.
notes: arXiv OA reproducibility-in-ML review.

title: Disparity between statistical and clinical significance in published trials
author: Sedgwick P. et al.
snippet: Documents the disparity between statistical and clinical significance in published trials, finding that many 'statistically significant' results are clinically trivial while some 'non-significant' results have meaningful effect sizes. Argues for confidence intervals and minimum clinically important differences (MCID).
notes: PMC meta-research paper bridging negative-findings and uncertainty gaps.

title: Statistical Considerations for Subgroup Analyses - PMC - NIH
author: Sedgwick P. et al.
snippet: PMC statistical considerations for subgroup analyses. Reviews pre-specification, interaction tests, multiplicity adjustment, and explicit cautions that subgroup findings are exploratory and restricted to pre-specified hypotheses. Emphasizes 'among participants meeting criterion X' framing.
notes: PMC subgroup-analysis methods paper — rich scope-qualifier language.

title: Three simple rules to ensure reasonably credible subgroup
author: Sun X., Briel M., Walter S. D., Guyatt G. H.
snippet: Sun et al.'s BMJ paper proposing three simple rules to ensure reasonably credible subgroup analyses. Rules include pre-specification, interaction testing, and replicability; paper repeatedly emphasizes that subgroup claims are restricted to the populations and conditions under which they were observed.
notes: Cite-~1500 BMJ methodology paper on credible subgroup analyses.

title: Tutorial on statistical considerations on subgroup analysis
author: Varadhan R., Weiss C. O., Segal J. B. et al.
snippet: Statistics in Medicine tutorial on statistical considerations for subgroup analysis. Covers effect modification versus interaction, conditional inference, and explicit warnings about restricting conclusions to 'the studied population and pre-specified subgroups' rather than the broader eligible population.
notes: Wiley Statistics in Medicine tutorial on subgroup analyses.

title: External validity, generalisability, applicability and directness - PubMed
author: Rehfuess E. A. et al.
snippet: PubMed abstract for a methods paper on external validity, generalisability, applicability and directness in evidence synthesis. Distinguishes internal validity (study quality) from external validity (applicability to target populations) and proposes structured frameworks for reporting scope limits.
notes: PubMed methods abstract on external validity — strong scope-qualifier reference.

title: Overview: Cohort Study Designs - PMC - NIH
author: Song J. W., Chung K. C.
snippet: PMC overview of cohort study designs (prospective, retrospective, ambidirectional). Discusses loss to follow-up, selection bias, and the importance of explicit reporting of 'among participants enrolled at baseline meeting eligibility criteria X' to define the scope of association estimates.
notes: PMC cohort-design overview — scope-qualifier patterns for observational claims.

title: The difference between I-squared and prediction intervals
author: Borenstein M. et al.
snippet: PubMed abstract for a methods paper explaining the difference between I-squared (a measure of heterogeneity proportion) and prediction intervals (which capture the range of true effects in new studies). Argues against conflating low I-squared with narrow prediction intervals.
notes: Methods abstract clarifying heterogeneity vs prediction intervals.

title: Beyond prediction intervals in meta-analysis: reporting the
author: IntHout J. et al.
snippet: Springer BMC Medical Research Methodology paper on reporting prediction intervals beyond standard confidence intervals in meta-analysis. Demonstrates that prediction intervals better convey expected effect variation in new populations; recommends paired reporting with CIs for transparent uncertainty communication.
notes: Springer OA paper on prediction-interval reporting in meta-analysis.

title: Chapter 10: Analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses
author: Deeks J. J., Higgins J. P. T., Altman D. G. (editors)
snippet: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 10 on analysing data and undertaking meta-analyses. Provides canonical guidance on effect measures, fixed versus random effects, confidence intervals, heterogeneity statistics (I-squared, tau-squared), and explicit uncertainty language conventions for Cochrane reviews.
notes: Cochrane Handbook Ch 10 — canonical meta-analysis methodology reference.

title: Chapter 6: Choosing effect measures and computing
author: Higgins J. P. T., Li T., Deeks J. J. (editors)
snippet: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 6 on choosing effect measures and computing estimates. Covers risk ratios, odds ratios, risk differences, mean differences; explains when each is appropriate; emphasises paired CI reporting and warns against transforming effect measures post hoc.
notes: Cochrane Handbook Ch 6 — effect-measure methodology.

title: Recommendations for examining and interpreting funnel plot asymmetry
author: Sterne J. A. C. et al.
snippet: Sterne et al. BMJ recommendations for examining and interpreting funnel plot asymmetry in meta-analyses. Provides guidance on when funnel-plot asymmetry indicates publication bias versus other artefacts, and recommends sensitivity analysis and contour-enhanced plots as uncertainty checks.
notes: Sterne et al. BMJ paper on funnel plot asymmetry.

title: Universal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Inference in
author: Goodman-Bacon A., Marcus M.
organization: PMC / NIH (Annual Review of Public Health)
snippet: PMC paper on 'Universal Difference-in-Differences for Causal Inference' extending DiD to settings with staggered treatment timing and heterogeneous effects. Discusses uncertainty quantification via bootstrapping, sensitivity to parallel-trends violations, and explicit scope limitations of DiD-derived causal estimates.
notes: PMC DiD methodology paper — bridges causal + uncertainty.

title: Mendelian randomization: use of genetics to enable causal  - PubMed
author: Burgess S., Thompson S. G.
snippet: PubMed abstract for a foundational Mendelian randomization review. Explains how genetic variants as instrumental variables enable causal inference from observational data, and discusses assumptions (relevance, exclusion restriction, independence) and uncertainty in weak-instrument settings.
notes: PubMed MR review abstract — bridges causal + uncertainty.

title: Synthesizing and presenting findings using other methods
author: McKenzie J. E., Brennan S. E. (editors)
snippet: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 12 on synthesizing and presenting findings using methods other than meta-analysis (e.g., vote counting, albatross plots, qualitative synthesis). Provides explicit guidance on calibrated uncertainty language ('may', 'probably', 'no evidence') per GRADE certainty tiers.
notes: Cochrane Handbook Ch 12 — calibrated uncertainty language.

title: PRISMA 2020 checklist
author: Page M. J. et al. (PRISMA Group)
snippet: PRISMA 2020 checklist (27-item reporting guideline for systematic reviews). Provides the canonical reporting framework including search strategy, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty-of-evidence grading, and explicit caveats about scope (population, intervention, comparator, outcomes) of included studies.
notes: PRISMA 2020 checklist — canonical systematic-review reporting standard.

title: The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting
author: Page M. J., McKenzie J. E., Bossuyt P. M. et al.
snippet: PubMed entry for the PRISMA 2020 statement published in BMJ 2021. The 27-item update of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses includes flow diagrams, search-strategy registration, and explicit reporting of scope, certainty, and limitations sections.
notes: PRISMA 2020 statement PubMed record.

title: Assessing risk of bias due to missing evidence in a meta-analysis
author: Page M. J., Higgins J. P. T., Sterne J. A. C. (editors)
snippet: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 13 on assessing risk of bias due to missing evidence (ROB-ME). Discusses publication bias, selective non-reporting, and P-hunting; provides explicit framework for grading down certainty of evidence when missing-evidence bias is suspected — direct EVIDENCE_LIMITATION coverage.
notes: Cochrane Handbook Ch 13 — bias due to missing evidence.

title: Including non-randomized studies on intervention effects
author: Sterne J. A. C., Hernán M. A., Reeves B. C. et al. (editors)
snippet: Cochrane Handbook Chapter 24 on including non-randomized studies on intervention effects (ROBINS-I tool). Provides structured assessment of confounding, selection, misclassification biases; emphasises that observational evidence is graded lower in certainty and explicitly scope-limited.
notes: Cochrane Handbook Ch 24 — ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies.

title: Finding What Works in Health Care: Standards for Systematic Reviews
author: Institute of Medicine (IOM) Committee on Standards for Systematic Reviews
snippet: National Academies consensus report 'Finding What Works in Health Care: Standards for Systematic Reviews'. Establishes 21 standards for systematic-review conduct, including explicit handling of scope, heterogeneity, publication bias, and GRADE certainty-of-evidence assessment across multi-page methodological chapters.
notes: National Academies systematic-review standards consensus report.

title: Methodological and reporting characteristics of Campbell reviews
author: White H. et al.
snippet: A systematic review of methodological and reporting characteristics of Campbell Collaboration systematic reviews. Documents how Campbell reviews in social/economic policy address heterogeneity, scope qualifiers, certainty-of-evidence reporting, and publication-bias assessment across multi-page evidence-synthesis reports.
notes: Campbell Collaboration meta-review — strong long-form coverage.

title: GRADE
author: Guyatt G. H. et al. (GRADE Working Group)
snippet: Cochrane methodology resource on GRADE — the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework. Defines four certainty tiers (high, moderate, low, very low) and explicit calibrated language for moving from evidence to recommendations, with structured handling of scope, indirectness, and imprecision.
notes: Cochrane GRADE methodology resource — canonical uncertainty + scope framework.
